newsitem.title: FINLAND: LIPPONEN SAYS FIM 9 BLN 1998-99 TAX CUTS TOO MUCH.
newsitem.headline: LIPPONEN SAYS FIM 9 BLN 1998-99 TAX CUTS TOO MUCH.

text.p: Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said on Wednesday income tax cuts worth nine billion markka in 1998-99 proposed by a group of senior economists would be too much.
"One must first ask how big (income tax) reductions the state finances can afford," Lipponen said in a television interview late on Wednesday evening.

"Of course tax relief is needed for wage earners across the board, and pensioners' must get their share as well ... (but) when the question is about a nine billion (markka) programme it is certainly overdimensioned," he said.
"I think the group has estimated, a bit optimistically, that half of the nine billion markka reduction would come back by itself," Lipponen said.
The economists' said the dynamic effects of increased activity would return around 50 percent of the public sector revenue shortfall from their proposed five percentage points income tax cut.
"Because it will not finance itself to the extent that these experts assume it means that it cannot be that big," Lipponen said, but did not make it clear how he knew the economists were wrong.
"And then there is the question whether there is reason to stimulate very much further by means of taxation when the economy is already growing so strongly," he said.
"When economic growth is strong incomes are rising anyway," he added.

"The government will in any case aim at income tax reductions during the latter half of the election period," Lipponen said, adding tax cuts prospects would depend on 1998 pay rises to be agreed next autumn by unions and employers.
"It is very positive that these experts unanimously agree that tax relief must be targetted at low-wage workers," he said.
"I am of the opinion that there is no reason to finance lower taxes by cutting unemployment security," Lipponen said.
"Now the important thing is to make it more advantageous for low-wage earners to go to work (than live off jobless benefits) and also for employers to hire people for low-wage jobs," he said.
